captions.text: Start with a query you already recognize.
Select the order identifier and total from orders, keep the rows whose status is paid, and return them
in identifier order.
We are not going to begin with definitions of databases or tuples.
We are going to follow this statement through PostgreSQL, and learn how to check what the engine really
did.
The goal is to make a habit: first decide what a query must mean, then inspect how the
database implements it, and only then decide whether a change improves it.
Correctness comes before speed.
Our example has three separate responsibilities.
The from clause names a relation.
The where clause says which rows belong in the result.
The select list says which values to return.
Order by adds an ordering guarantee.
Without order by, the engine owes you the right rows but not a particular sequence.
A physical plan is allowed to arrange work differently from the order of words in the statement.
This freedom is the reason SQL can be optimized.
It is also the reason guessing execution from the spelling of a query often leads you astray.
The client sends SQL text to PostgreSQL over a connection.
Before the database can search for any orders, it must recognize the statement.
Lexing recognizes tokens such as select, a column identifier, and a string literal.
Parsing checks that these tokens form a valid statement and builds a syntax tree.
A misspelled keyword or an unmatched parenthesis can stop the journey here.
Notice what a syntax error does not tell you: it tells you nothing about the efficiency of an
index or the speed of storage, because no order rows have been retrieved yet.
Analysis connects the syntax to database objects.
Which orders table does this name refer to?
Does the identifier column exist?
What is the type of total?
Which equality operator should compare status with the string paid?
PostgreSQL resolves these questions using its catalogs, namespace rules and type system.
It also checks relevant permissions.
A statement can be grammatical and still fail analysis because a column does not exist.
The type of an expression matters later too.
Casting an indexed value or applying a function can change which access paths are available.
We will investigate those cases with real indexes in later chapters.
Next comes rewriting.
A view can stand for a stored query whose definition must be expanded.
Rules and security policies can add or transform expressions before planning.
The important idea is that the planner may receive a richer representation than the short SQL text the
client sent.
In this first lab the orders table is a plain relation and no special rewrite is needed.
The illustrated journey still includes this stage so you can place more complex behavior correctly when we introduce
views and row level security.
An animation shows the mechanism; it is not a recording of every instruction in the server.
The planner considers ways to produce the required result.
It can read a table sequentially, probe an index, or combine access paths.
It can obtain order from a suitable index or add a sort.
To compare alternatives, it uses estimates about the number of rows, the distribution of values, and the cost
of work.
Estimates are not measurements of this execution.
The planner's costs are also not milliseconds.
They are relative cost units used to choose among alternatives.
A lower estimated cost can be informative, but it is not a stopwatch and does not prove the
actual query is faster.
For a tiny orders table, a sequential scan is often entirely reasonable.
Reading a handful of pages can be cheaper than traversing an index and fetching heap rows individually.
The primary key on identifier does not imply that every query should use it.
We will use much larger and differently distributed fixtures later so you can see the crossover.
Good optimization asks which method fits the required rows and the workload.
It does not grade every sequential scan as a failure.
A plan choice that is excellent for one tenant or parameter can be poor for another.
The executor runs the selected plan.
Think of the root asking its child for the next result, and the request moving down toward a
scan.
The scan reads candidates and checks the filter.
It emits only matching rows.
A sort may have to consume all of its input before it can return the first ordered row.
Projection computes the requested values, and the result travels back to the client.
The stream of illustrated dots represents this pull based mechanism.
It is a teaching model, not a per row trace captured by explain.
Real measurements will be shown separately in the plan panel.
Now use Explain in the workbench.
This asks PostgreSQL for a plan without running the query.
Read from the leaves upward to understand where rows originate and how operators transform them.
Then use Analyze.
Explain analyze really executes the statement and collects execution statistics.
In this chapter your learner role can only read the fixture, so a destructive command cannot change it.
In later mutation labs, analyze can perform writes and will run only in disposable exercise environments.
Never assume that adding explain analyze makes an arbitrary statement harmless.
Compare estimated rows with actual rows at the scan.
A large mismatch is a clue about selectivity estimates, not automatically proof that an index is missing.
Notice rows removed by the filter and the sort's input and output.
Counts reported by a node with multiple loops are per loop, so you must interpret them with the
loop count.
Upper node times and buffer counters can include work beneath them.
Do not add every node's numbers and claim that is the total cost.
Parallel execution makes naive subtraction even less reliable.
We will practice these details repeatedly before the advanced optimizer chapters.
There is one more correctness trap in this small example.
Null means the value is unknown.
Comparing a total with null using equals does not produce true.
Use is null when you want unknown totals.
Descending order puts nulls first by default, so a top three query may return unknown amounts unless you
state the intended policy.
A tie also needs a deterministic second key if the exercise asks for a particular order.
These choices are part of the result contract.
A faster query that changes them is a different query, even when the visible sample happens to look
the same.
Complete the six exercises after this video.
First find paid orders, then handle an unknown total, make a strict amount boundary precise, choose the top
three deterministically, project an exact discount, and reconcile matched rows with an aggregate.
The grader runs fresh fixture variants, so hardcoding the visible identifiers or adding an accidental limit will not
establish correctness.
You can run as often as you like.
A first submitted attempt unlocks the collapsed explanation even when the query has a syntax error.
Reading that explanation does not mark the question passed.
Every required question must pass before the next chapter opens.
Keep this loop for the rest of the course: define the result, observe the engine, form a hypothesis,
change one thing, and verify both correctness and measured work.
